newsitem.title: INDIA: India market seen hit by worry on politics, reform.
newsitem.headline: India market seen hit by worry on politics, reform.

text.p: A steep fall in Indian stock markets this week has stirred debate over whether India's attractiveness as an emerging market is being eroded by political worries and fears free-market reforms may be reversed.
"Indian opportunities are not seen as good as Southeast Asia, Latin America or East Europe," Ian Allison, head of sales at brokerage firm Caspian Securities, said on Wednesday.
"When domestic funds and retail investors are shunning the market, FIIs (foreign institutional investors) will inevitably get scared," Allison said. FIIs are major investors in India.
On Tuesday, the benchmark 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index edged up 24.49 points to close at 3,027.35 after plunging 98.41 points on Monday.
Traders expect Tuesday's weak rebound to be short-lived.
"Interest has tapered off to some extent," said P. Singaravelu, research manager at First India Asset Management, which manages a country fund dedicated to Indian equities.
A European fund manager, who declined to be identified, said a number of developments have triggered fears of a reversal of economic reforms under India's new government.
He cited the government's decision at the weekend to disallow a joint venture domestic airline planned by India's Tata group and Singapore Airlines.

India's minister for aviation C.M. Ibrahim was quoted by newspapers as saying Jet Airways, the only Indian carrier with with foreign shareholders, would be asked to terminate agreements by which Gulf Air and Kuwait Airways have acquired a combined 40 percent stake.

The Business Standard newspaper on Tuesday reported Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, in a speech in New Delhi, "heaped scorn on the economic liberalisation policy initiated by the previous Congress government, saying that it had brought no benefits to the poor and the common man."
"Those who believe economic liberalisation will usher in a miracle are either living in a fool's paradise or else trying to mislead the countrymen," it quoted him as saying.
The future of Deve Gowda's government, in power since June, is itself in doubt following a threat by the Congress party to withdraw support for the minority ruling coalition.

But some analysts said the gloom triggered by the free fall in share prices was unwarranted. Aditya Samant, economist at UBS Securities in Hong Kong, said the stock market plunge was not justified by the country's economic fundamentals.
"It is an illogical movement which could get reversed," he said. "The problem is people are getting too pessimistic. The economy is doing better than what most people think."
M.R. Madhavan, research manager at ICICI Securities and Finance Company, said preliminary data on industrial production growth did not necessarily bode ill for the economy.
"Overall growth won't be bad this year," he said.
